PET Evidence of Central
GABAergic Changes in Stiff-
Person Syndrome
Daniela Perani, MD, 1,2* Valentina Garibotto, MD, 2,3
Andrea Panzacchi, MD, 2,4
Rosa Maria Moresco, MSc, 2,3,4 Paola Ortelli, MSc, 2
Massimo Corbo, MD, 5 Ferruccio Fazio, MD, 2,3,4
and Franco Folli, MD 6
1Istituto Nazionale di Neuroscienze, Vita-Salute San Raffaele
University, Milan, Italy; 2Scientiﬁc Institute San Raffaele,
Department of Nuclear Medicine, Milan, Italy; 3Milano-
Bicocca University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Milan,
Italy; 4Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche, Istituto di
Bioimmagini e Fisiologia Molecolare, Milan, Italy;
5University of Milan Medical School, IRCCS Istituto
Auxologico Italiano, Department of Neurology, Milan, Italy;
6Division of Diabetes, Department of Medicine, University of
Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio, Texas, USA
Abstract: We measured expression of central nervous sys-
tem GABA-A receptors with 11C-ﬂumazenil ( 11C-FMZ)
and PET in two subjects with stiff person syndrome (SPS).
We found reduced 11C-FMZ binding potential (BP) in mo -
tor-premotor cortex, and increased 11C-FMZ BP in the
cerebellar nuclei. This is the ﬁrst in vivo PET evidence of
central GABA-A receptors dysfunction in SPS, possibly
concurring to the motor symptoms. © 2007 Movement Dis-
order Society
Key words: positron emission tomography; stiff person syn-
drome;
11C-ﬂumazenil; GABA.
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare and disabling
disorder characterized by muscle rigidity and episodic
spasms involving the axial and limb musculature.
1 The
cause of SPS is unknown, but an autoimmune pathogen-
esis has been proposed on the basis of the presence of
antiglutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies in the
serum and in the CSF,
2 the association with other auto-
immune disorders and autoantibodies, and the response
to immunotherapies.
3 Recently, in vivo MRI spectros-
copy showed a prominent and signiﬁcant decrease in
GABA level in the sensorimotor cortex.
4
These data were presented at the 58th Meeting of the American
Academy of Neurology, 2006, and published in Abstract form, Neu-
rology, vol. 66 (S2), page A134.
*Correspondence to: Daniela Perani, Vita-Salute San Raffaele Uni-
versity, Via Olgettina 60, 20132 Milan, Italy.
E-mail: daniela.perani@hsr.it
Received 9 October 2006; Revised 16 January 2007; Accepted 18
January 2007
Published online 7 March 2007 in Wiley InterScience (www.
interscience.wiley.com). DOI: 10.1002/mds.21441
1030 D. PERANI ET AL.
Movement Disorders, Vol. 22, No. 7, 2007
Aim of this study is to explore the GABAergic system
in vivo by using PET and the central GABA-A receptors
linked benzodiazepine binding sites antagonist
11C-
ﬂumazenil ( 11C-FMZ) as a ligand.
METHODS
Clinical Characteristics of the Patients
Subject 1 is a 45-year-old man affected by type 1
diabetes mellitus, complaining of leg proximal rigidity
and falls; symptoms ameliorated by using diazepam. On
the basis of clinical history and laboratory data (Table 1),
a diagnosis of SPS and epilepsy was done.
Subject 2 is a 53-year-old woman; her medical history
was notable for onset of vitiligo at age 33, Graves’
disease at age 38, and type 1 diabetes mellitus at age 51.
At age 52 she began complaining of muscle rigidity,
cramps, and painful spasms. These symptoms involved
mainly the axial musculature, but also the proximal por-
tion of lower and upper limbs, and were partially ame-
liorated by low doses of diazepam. On the basis of
clinical and laboratory examinations (Table 1), a diag-
nosis of probable SPS was made. She also presented
severe anxiety symptoms (sudden heart pulsations, dif-
fused perspiration, sense of suffocation, general trem-
bling, and vertigo), resembling panic attacks. She had
high scores on the HARS scale (clinically signiﬁcant
anxiety).
5
Clinical and Laboratory Assessment
The two patients underwent complete medical, neuro-
logical, and electrophysiological investigations, in asso-
ciation with laboratory testing (listed in Table 1). A
formal psychiatric evaluation was performed to detect
and quantify disorders commonly associated with SPS,
namely anxiety and depression, together with an exten-
sive neuropsychological battery, which included global
screening test and evaluation of language, memory,
visuospatial abilities, and executive functions.
6
11C-FMZ PET
The studies were performed with an 18-ring whole-
body PET scanner (GE Advance, General Electric Med-
ical System, Milwaukee, WI). Acquisition protocols and
images analysis were performed according to methods
previously described.
7 We obtained parametric images
for binding potential (BP), representing in vivo radioli-
gand binding under conditions of trace receptor occu-
pancy, and parametric images of relative
11C-FMZ K1
(termed RI), reﬂecting brain perfusion; we used RI im-
ages to check for the presence of perfusion deﬁcits.
Reconstructed images were analyzed using Statistical
parametric mapping, SPM2.8 11C-FMZ BP spatially nor -
malized images of each patient were compared with a
group of nine male healthy subjects (mean age: 26 /H110063;
range: 23 to 32 years) previously collected in our depart-
ment.
7 This control group is younger than the patients;
however PET studies using this tracer showed its invari-
ance over age.
9 Statistical threshold was set at P /H110210.01.
RESULTS
Neuropsychological Evaluation
Subject 1 scored within normal ranges in all the ex-
plored cognitive domains, while Subject 2 showed deﬁ-
cits in executive functions, namely working memory,
problem solving, and categorizing.
PET Results
SPM-2 analysis of
11C-FMZ PET data in the two SPS
subjects, as compared with normal controls, revealed a
signiﬁcant and extensive reduction of 11C-FMZ BP in the
premotor cortex, bilaterally. There was also a partial involve-
ment of the motor cortex and the right supplementary motor

conﬁned to the cerebellar nuclei (Table 2 and Fig. 1).
The two subject’s RI maps did not show any signiﬁ-
cant alteration of brain perfusion in these areas, when
compared with normal controls.
With the aim of providing some preliminary, explor-
ative data in a rare disorder, we also performed a single
subject analysis that revealed in Subject 2, the patient
reporting anxiety disorders,
11C-FMZ BP reductions in
the amygdala complex, bilaterally.
DISCUSSION
This is the ﬁrst 11C-FMZ PET study in SPS, showing
changes in central GABA-A receptors linked benzodiaz-
epine binding sites in selected brain regions. This is also
consistent with recent MRI spectroscopy data.
4
The decreases in 11C-FMZ BP might be explained as
(1) a direct consequence of the reduction in GABA
levels, followed by a downregulation of the receptors, in
chronic patients; (2) local and selective alterations of the
subunit composition of the GABA-A complex, related to
the SPS disease process; (3) focal dysfunctions, how-
ever, not supported by regional perfusion changes; (4)
focal atrophy that would need further evaluations using
unbiased voxel-based methods.
Our data support the view that SPS is also a central
disorder; a regional decrease in GABA tone in the pre-
motor–motor cortex may impair the action of inhibitory
pathways, contributing to muscle rigidity and spasms.
The evidence of a reduced
11C-FMZ BP also in limbic
structures, in the patient with anxiety disorders, is com-
parable with the signiﬁcant reduction found in patients
with panic disorder.
10
The selective GABAergic involvement of premotor–
motor and limbic cortices might be due to the high
demand of modulator control in these regions, based on
their ﬁnely tuned GABAergic transmission.
11
As for the relative increase of 11C-FMZ BP in the
cerebellar nuclei, it may be related to an upregulation of
the GABA cerebellar system control, compensating for
the reduction of GABA neurotransmitter at the motor
level.
We are aware that these data represent just a prelim-
inary, descriptive report in a rare disorder. More evi-
dences, coming from further molecular, functional, and
structural studies, will help in explaining the pathophys-
iology of SPS.
